children: Indian IT stocks jumped sharply on Tuesday, tracking a broader recovery in global software shares after leading artificial intelligence executives called for a more measured pace of AI development amid growing concerns over its risks and potential misuse.

The Indian IT index rose as much as 5.2 per cent, putting it on course for its strongest session since 2 July. The gains came after a prolonged sell-off that has pushed the sector down about 21 per cent this year, more than twice the decline in the benchmark Nifty 50.

Indian IT companies have been under pressure as investors assess the potential for AI to disrupt traditional outsourcing models. The country's roughly $315 billion IT industry has been considered particularly exposed because of its longstanding dependence on billing based on employee hours.
Analysts said a slower pace of AI advancement could provide Indian technology companies with more time to adapt their business models and manage investments in new technologies.

“A slower pace of AI development could give Indian IT firms more time to adapt to new models and manage their costs,” said Piyush Pandey, an analyst at Centrum Broking. He described Tuesday's move as a tactical rebound rather than evidence of a fundamental turnaround in the sector.
HCLTech led gains, rising 6.21 per cent after eight consecutive sessions of losses. Infosys climbed 4.72 per cent, while TCS gained 4.76 per cent.

The rally followed comments from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who urged AI companies to slow the pace at which they increase the capabilities of their models amid concerns about the technology's potential misuse. xAI chief Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman have also expressed agreement with the call for greater caution.
Concerns about the potential risks of AI intensified earlier this month after Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned, arguing that AI companies were taking excessive risks with the technology.

Meanwhile, Indian IT outsourcing giants including TCS, Infosys, Wipro and HCLTech are reshaping their business models in response to AI-driven disruption. Companies are increasingly moving towards performance- and outcome-based pricing rather than billing clients primarily for hours worked, as customers seek lower costs and higher productivity.
